Geometric queries and acceleration structures

A ray exactly on a shared edge can be inconsistently classified by floating-point arithmetic, so robust tests need a consistent edge rule or conservative predicates. CMU-12

Closest-point queries project a point onto a triangle plane, then clamp to the appropriate edge or vertex when the projection is outside the face. Signed distance adds a sign indicating inside versus outside, often determined by orientation or a winding test. These queries occur in collision detection, surface reconstruction, and modeling. The mathematical answer should be independent of the data structure used to accelerate it. CMU-12

Naively testing a ray against every triangle costs operations for faces. A bounding-volume hierarchy groups primitives inside boxes. A ray-box slab test computes an interval of possible ray parameters for each coordinate axis; intersect the three intervals, rejecting when their common interval is empty. If a ray is parallel to a slab and its origin is outside, reject; if inside, that axis imposes no extra restriction. The bound must be conservative: a false positive costs time, but a false negative loses a real hit. CMU-13

BVH traversal descends only into boxes hit by the ray. Visiting the nearer child first can find a closest hit early; any later node whose nearest possible hit is farther can be pruned. A shadow query can stop at its first blocker, while a transparent visibility query may need several hits. Uniform grids, k-d trees, and BVHs suit different geometry distributions and update patterns. A BVH can be refit after small motion or rebuilt for tighter bounds. Acceleration changes the cost, not the result, of a query. CMU-13
Bounding-volume hierarchy invariants

A BVH is a tree. Every leaf contains one or more primitives; every interior node has children whose primitive sets partition its own. The children’s boxes may overlap spatially, but a primitive belongs to only one child set. A node bound encloses every descendant primitive. This containment property ensures that a ray missing a node cannot hit any geometry below it. The split heuristic affects speed, not correctness. A surface-area heuristic estimates expected traversal cost by balancing the cost of testing a node against the probability that a ray visits a child.

For an axis-aligned box with coordinate bounds , a ray coordinate is . If , the slab-entry and exit parameters are and . If , their ordering reverses. Taking the maximum of entry parameters and minimum of exit parameters across axes gives the intersection interval. The ray hits if the interval is nonempty and overlaps allowed values. Parallel components require explicit treatment to avoid division by zero. Floating-point implementations often use reciprocal directions and precomputed sign bits, but must preserve conservative behavior near boundaries. CMU-13

Dynamic geometry can update a BVH by refitting node boxes from child bounds. Refit preserves correctness but can leave poor partitions after large deformation. Rebuilding costs more immediately but may produce tighter bounds and faster future traversal. If a scene receives many rays between updates, rebuilding can pay off; for rapidly changing scenes with few rays, a quick refit may be preferable. This is a workload decision. CMU-13
Data structures shape the algorithm

A uniform grid maps each primitive to intersected cells. Ray traversal steps cell by cell, but a large primitive may occupy many cells and produce duplicate tests. A k-d tree partitions space with planes; splitting a primitive can require storing it in multiple leaves. A BVH partitions primitives into disjoint sets while allowing spatially overlapping bounds. This is especially useful when objects are clustered or empty space is irregular. Different acceleration structures are not interchangeable abstractions in performance terms, though each should produce the same geometric answer.

The choice of query and structure should be tested against expected rays. Primary camera rays tend to be coherent; neighboring rays point in similar directions. Shadow rays point toward light sources. Diffuse bounce rays are more scattered. A structure optimized for one ray distribution may perform differently for another. This is a general systems lesson: data structures encode assumptions about future queries. CMU-13
Robustness and conditioning are related but different

Conditioning describes how sensitive the exact mathematical answer is to input changes. Algorithmic stability describes whether a numerical method adds additional error beyond that sensitivity. Nearly parallel line intersection is ill-conditioned: a tiny angular change can move the intersection far away. Higher precision cannot make the geometric problem well-conditioned, but a stable method can avoid making it worse. For a well-conditioned problem, a numerically unstable method can still return a poor answer. Robust geometry needs both an understanding of conditioning and careful arithmetic.

Orientation predicates, such as determining whether one point lies to the left or right of a directed edge, often reduce to the sign of a determinant. Near zero, roundoff can flip the sign, causing inconsistent topology decisions. Adaptive precision evaluates cheaply in ordinary cases and uses more precision only when the result is uncertain. Such predicates matter in triangulation, ray-edge tests, and mesh repair. The point is not to eliminate all floating-point error; it is to prevent uncertain local calculations from violating global invariants. CMU-12 · CMU-13
Acceleration: spend scene work once so each ray can skip most geometry

A ray tracer’s brute-force inner loop compares each ray with every primitive. With image samples, triangles, and an average of rays generated per sample (including shadow and secondary rays), a crude work model is . If an object contains triangles, a bounding-volume miss can save all triangle tests for that ray. The bounding volume must be conservative: it may contain extra empty space, but it cannot exclude any part of the object. A loose bound wastes work; a costly, tight bound can cost more than it saves. Construction is amortized across queries: if setup costs and it saves work per ray, it becomes worthwhile after about rays. This changes for a deforming animated object, where bounds may need refitting or rebuilding each frame; a wider bound can instead cover several poses at the cost of weaker culling. If one direction component is zero, the ray is parallel to that pair of slab planes: it misses if its origin lies outside the slab, otherwise that axis places no bound on . This is the slab method and it reduces an AABB query to a few min/max operations. A triangle bound is formed by coordinatewise minima/maxima of its three vertices; a sphere centered at with radius has bounds . An infinite plane has no useful finite AABB. MITG-12 (00:20:30–00:30:00)

A bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) groups primitives under a tree of conservative boxes. Each primitive belongs to one leaf, while sibling boxes may overlap. Each internal node has the bound of its descendants. To query, intersect a node box; if it misses, discard the entire subtree. If it hits, visit its children, then test primitives in reached leaves. The data structure is useful only when bounds prune enough work: a camera inside a single bunny-sized box, or a million identical triangles, may yield little improvement. Simple split rules divide a list in half, sort by centroid and take the median, or reuse an artist’s modeling hierarchy. The lecture stresses that the common constructions are heuristics, not a proof of traversal. A balanced-looking tree can still overlap heavily or be poorly aligned to actual rays. MITG-12 (00:30:00–00:38:30; 00:45:45–00:46:40)

A BVH must not stop merely because it finds a primitive in the first child box it intersects. Sibling boxes can overlap: a ray may enter the right sibling’s box first, hit a primitive geometrically assigned to that box, and still encounter a nearer primitive assigned to the left sibling. The safe general rule is to examine all candidate children, retain the least valid , and prune only when a node’s near bound is farther than the best hit already found. The BVH stores each object once, so avoiding duplicate primitive tests costs little memory. MITG-12 (00:38:30–00:46:40)

A -d tree makes a different trade. It partitions space with axis-aligned split planes, so the cells do not overlap, but a triangle crossing a split may be stored in both children. A node records the split axis, split coordinate, and front/back children or leaf primitives. This avoids overlapping spatial regions and enables near-to-far traversal, at the expense of duplicated storage and possibly repeated primitive tests. There is no universal construction rule: splitting the world cell in half can leave one child full and one almost empty; splitting by median primitive centroid balances counts but not necessarily ray cost. The surface area heuristic (SAH) estimates traversal cost from the areas of candidate child regions and the number of primitives assigned to them, reflecting the likelihood that rays visit those regions. It is a useful engineering heuristic rather than a guarantee. MITG-12 (00:46:40–00:54:10; 01:01:45–01:05:10)

Traversal correctness comes from parameter intervals. At a node, let the parent region be intersected by the ray over . Find the ray parameter at the split plane. If , the ray reaches only the back child in this interval. If , it reaches only the front child. Otherwise it reaches both; determine which is near from the ray direction, recurse into that child over its subinterval first, and search the far child only if no valid hit was found before . A primitive duplicated into both cells may have a geometric hit outside the current cell interval; reject such a hit here, or the first cell could report a surface that lies beyond the split and incorrectly hide a nearer object. The parent bounds and inherited interval are therefore not bookkeeping trivia—they are what make early termination safe. MITG-12 (00:50:45–01:01:30)

A regular grid provides another organization. Insert each primitive into every cell its bound or geometry overlaps. Traverse the cells in the order the ray crosses them and test only their contents. The 3D digital differential analyzer (DDA) keeps the next crossing parameter for each axis. From current cell entry , advance to the smallest next boundary time, update the corresponding cell index, and update that axis’s next time by a constant increment. For example, if the next x face is at and the next y face is at , advance y first; then compare the updated times again. Stop once a valid primitive hit lies within the current cell’s interval. A primitive spanning several cells can be tested repeatedly unless the implementation marks already-tested primitives. Tiny cells increase walking overhead; large cells put many primitives in each bucket. Uniform grids suit scenes with roughly uniform object scale, and their ordered loops can be simpler to parallelize than recursive trees. MITG-12 (01:09:20–01:18:50)

Visibility: compare depth locally or trace paths

After projection, screen x and y say where a sample lands; depth says which opaque surface is in front. A depth buffer stores one depth per pixel next to the color buffer. When a triangle rasterizes a pixel, interpolate its depth and compare it with the stored value. If the new fragment is nearer, replace both color and stored depth; otherwise leave the current pixel alone. This makes the result independent of the order in which opaque triangles were submitted and reduces to a local comparison that GPUs can perform in parallel. (P3-07)

The comparison direction and clear value are paired with the chosen depth mapping. In this lecture’s image-space convention, near is larger than far, so it initializes to a very negative value and keeps the larger depth. In a common modern window-depth setup, nearer values are smaller, the buffer is cleared to 1, and a LESS test keeps the smaller value. Reversing one part without the other makes occlusion wrong. Perspective depth is nonlinear after divide: depth values are crowded toward the far end, so a needlessly tiny near distance relative to the far distance reduces precision. (P3-05–07)

A depth buffer solves visibility for opaque samples, not every light-transport problem. Transparent surfaces need blending and ordering or a different method; a single nearest-surface value cannot represent multiple layers. A shadow asks what is hidden from a light, while the camera depth test asks what is hidden from the eye. These are separate visibility queries. (P3-07)

Ray tracing asks the visibility question differently. For each pixel sample, cast a primary ray from the eye through the image plane, intersect it with scene objects, and keep the nearest hit. A naïve implementation costs about for pixel samples and objects. As a scale check, one million pixels times one thousand objects is roughly one billion intersection tests. A ray-sphere test can reduce to distance from the ray to the sphere center; triangles need a ray-triangle intersection test. Each pixel ray can be processed independently, but a straightforward implementation may perform much more work than rasterization.

Secondary rays add effects: send a shadow ray from a surface point toward a light and mark it shadowed if another object is encountered first; send a reflected ray in the mirror direction; send a refracted/transmitted ray through transparent material. Recursive effects can branch, so realism brings a potentially large cost. This is the geometric-optics view of light paths traced backward from the eye. The lecture contrasts its cost with the practical depth-buffer solution and previews later ray-tracing work. (P3-07)

Painter’s algorithm sorts surfaces back-to-front and draws them in order, but cyclic overlap can make a global ordering impossible unless geometry is split. A Warnock-style algorithm handles a complex screen region by subdividing it into four smaller regions and repeating until each region is simple enough to resolve. These methods illustrate different ways to turn a global visibility problem into a useful order or smaller local problems. (P3-07)

Chapter.Content: A painter’s algorithm is like painting distant scenery first and nearer objects over it. If every polygon can be placed in one back-to-front list, later drawing hides earlier color. Intersecting polygons can form a cycle—A in front of B in one region, B in front of C elsewhere, C in front of A—so there is no global scalar sort that works. A binary space partition (BSP) tree chooses a polygon plane, classifies other polygons against it, and splits polygons that cross. The tree stores an ordering, and traversal visits the far subtree, the node polygon, and the near subtree; which subtree is “far” depends on the camera’s side of the plane. Bounding volumes can avoid unnecessary split tests. A badly chosen splitter produces a deep, unbalanced tree and many tiny fragments, so random or heuristic plane selection can help. (P3-07, P3-14)

Warnock’s method works in screen space. For a viewport region, collect the polygons that overlap it. If there are none, leave it blank; if one surface alone determines the region, draw it; if a nearer polygon covers the whole region (a surrounder), discard surfaces hidden behind it. Otherwise divide the rectangle into four child windows and repeat with smaller polygon lists. At a one-pixel region, choose the nearest candidate; subdividing below pixel size and averaging samples improves edge coverage. This is a quadtree. Its tasks can be sent to separate processors, which explains why its recursive subdivision remains useful even when the original algorithm is not the main renderer. (P3-14)

The methods are complementary. Rasterization still needs coverage and interpolated attributes; the depth test chooses visible opaque samples. A BSP or painter order can avoid a per-pixel depth store in special geometry, but incurs scene sorting and splitting. Ray tracing resolves nearest intersections per ray and naturally adds secondary visibility queries. The lecture also mentions scanline/depth hybrids. Do not read the historical claim “this algorithm is dead” as a timeless API fact: hardware shifts the balance, and components of older methods reappear inside newer parallel renderers. (P3-14)
Ray intersection, recursive paths, and acceleration
A ray is an origin and direction : for . Normalize if you want to measure distance. For a plane through point with normal , an intersection lies on both the ray and plane, so

If , the ray is parallel; if it also lies in the plane, the intersection is non-unique and must be handled separately. Reject negative t because those hits lie behind the ray origin. This dot-product formula is the same signed-plane test used for clipping, now used to find a location rather than classify a whole endpoint. (P3-15)

For a sphere centered at with radius , let and let be unit length. Project V onto the ray with . The squared perpendicular distance is . If this exceeds , the ray misses. Otherwise its roots are and . Keep the smallest nonnegative root. This geometric derivation shows why spheres are an easy primitive, though a production implementation can solve the quadratic directly and must consider floating-point tolerances. For a triangle, intersect its plane and test the hit’s barycentric coordinates; all three coordinates must be nonnegative and sum to one. (P3-15)

A recursive Whitted-style renderer starts with the camera ray and shades the nearest surface. For each point light, cast a shadow ray toward it; a hit before the light means the direct source is blocked. For a reflective surface, reflect the incoming direction about the normal and trace a new ray; for a dielectric surface, use its refractive index and Snell’s law to trace transmission, with total internal reflection as an edge case. Add each returned radiance scaled by the material’s reflective/transmissive coefficient. Stop at a maximum bounce depth or when contribution becomes negligible, otherwise repeated mirrors can recurse indefinitely. The source transcript says “Turner Whitted”; the correct author is Turner Whitted, whose 1980 paper describes the recursive ray tree (ACM record, paper copy). (P3-07, P3-15)

Backward ray tracing traces from the eye because only paths contributing to visible pixels matter. It efficiently handles direct shadows and ideal mirror/refraction chains. It can miss a narrow light path that does not begin at the camera ray, such as a caustic where a lamp reflects from a mirror onto a diffuse table. Forward light tracing marks where emitted paths land; combining sampling strategies is harder but recovers such paths. Diffuse interreflection requires many scattered directions, so each surface hit can spawn many more rays. More rays improve coverage but increase work. This is the geometric-optics model, not a wave-optics simulation. (P3-15)

The naïve primary-ray cost is roughly primitive tests for samples and objects. Spatial acceleration groups objects. An octree recursively divides 3D space into eight cells; a ray visits only cells it crosses and tests the objects stored there. A kd-tree uses axis-aligned plane splits, often at adaptive positions rather than the exact center. Smaller leaves reduce primitive tests but increase tree traversal and storage. Objects crossing cell boundaries may be referenced in multiple nodes or handled by a spatial split rule. The ray-versus-cell traversal resembles grid line rasterization because both increment through ordered cells. (P3-15)

Implicit surfaces give another difficulty. If a surface is , substitute the ray coordinates to obtain , a one-variable root-finding problem. A quadratic can be solved directly; a generic polynomial of degree five or more has no general formula in radicals. Numerical root-finding is needed for many implicit surfaces. Neighboring pixel rays usually hit nearby points, so the previous ray’s root can seed the next search, but at silhouettes a tiny screen shift may jump to a different branch or miss the surface. This is why ray tracing a sphere or triangle is straightforward while ray tracing a high-order freeform surface is a numerical-analysis problem. (P3-15)

Hierarchies separate reusable local structure from global pose, allowing articulated surfaces to follow moving skeletons.
Forward kinematics makes inverse kinematics differentiable

A rig is a hierarchy of segments and joints. Forward kinematics starts at a root and composes each joint transform down the hierarchy to compute the position of a hand, foot, or other end effector. For a two-link planar chain with root , local segment vectors , and joint angles , let be the 2D rotation matrix. Then

The second rotation is relative to the first segment, so rotating the root joint also moves every child. Equivalently in the plane, rotations can be written as multiplication by complex numbers , where .

Inverse kinematics reverses the question. Rather than specifying joint angles and asking where the hand goes, specify a target and ask which angles place the hand there. For a target , one simple objective is

The Jacobian is the matrix of endpoint derivatives with respect to joint angles. The chain rule combines it with the residual to get a gradient, which can drive gradient descent. A character rig applies the same idea to many joints: asking the hand to reach a prop allows an optimizer to coordinate the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and torso. Joint limits, balance, and pose preferences can be added as constraints or penalties. Different configurations may reach the same target, and a target beyond the limb’s reach cannot achieve zero error, so the solver’s returned pose is a best feasible fit, not necessarily a unique or globally ideal artistic pose. CMU-22
Why linear blends can twist a character limb

Suppose one bone transform rotates a vertex +90 degrees and another rotates it -90 degrees. A naïve matrix blend at equal weights can approach a collapsed matrix rather than a halfway rotation. Applied to vertices along a limb, this can create a candy-wrapper twist or volume loss. A better rotation interpolation preserves the group structure of rotations, for example by quaternion interpolation, while translation or stretch is blended separately. This is one reason a transformation representation must reflect the object being interpolated. CMU-05 · CMU-06
Scene graphs: reuse local structure, compute global pose

A scene graph represents a complex object as a hierarchy of local coordinate frames. A robot arm is a useful abstract model: the forearm is positioned relative to the upper arm; the hand is positioned relative to the forearm. If the parent is moved or rotated, every descendant follows automatically. For a node with local transform , its world transform is

The ordering is the whole point: local transforms are composed along the path from root to node. A tree can reuse one definition of a hand or wheel and place it in multiple poses. It also provides a natural animation state: joint parameters modify local transforms, and traversal computes the consequences. The lecture explores hierarchical modeling, multiplying transforms along the graph, and inverse-kinematics questions such as choosing joint angles to place an endpoint MITG-05 (00:10:00–00:25:00; 00:35:00–00:50:00).
Each edge in the tree has a local transform, and a node’s world transform is the product of all edge transforms from the root. For a torso, shoulder, elbow, and wrist, for instance,

The wrist mesh can be authored once in wrist-local coordinates and transformed by this product. If the shoulder rotates, the elbow and wrist move because their world transforms inherit that factor; the wrist’s own local geometry does not need to be rewritten. A useful tree drawing is: world → torso → left upper arm → left forearm → left hand; the right arm is a second child branch. This is also why a scene graph is a reuse structure, not just a list of objects. An instanced chair can reuse a single chair mesh under several chair-to-world transforms. A character’s parts use parent-child transforms that encode attachment. The 2021 lecture gives the nested arm/hand/finger example and describes matrix push/pop as a traversal technique: descend while accumulating transforms, then restore the parent’s transform when returning to a sibling branch MITG-04 · MITG-05 (00:53:20–00:54:33; , 00:02:14–00:04:46).

Rotation around a joint requires one more composition detail. A rotation matrix rotates around its own origin, so a forearm joint displaced from the local origin needs : move the pivot to the origin, rotate, then move it back. With column vectors, the rightmost operation happens first. Forgetting either translation makes the bone spin around the model origin rather than bend at the elbow. This same “translate to pivot, rotate, translate back” pattern appears in mechanical parts, doors, and wheels.

An inverse-kinematics (IK) problem reverses the usual direction of evaluation. Forward kinematics says, “given joint values, where is the hand?” IK says, “given a target for the hand, what joint values reach it?” There may be many solutions, no exact solution, or solutions that violate joint constraints. Even a two-link planar arm makes the geometry clear: with lengths , a target at distance is reachable only when . Animation then needs a policy to choose among valid poses, such as smoothness over time or a preferred bend direction. A hierarchy supplies the forward model; solving for a pose is a separate optimization problem.

The Jacobian contains the partial derivative of each end-effector coordinate with respect to each joint parameter. Solve , update the joint values, and repeat. Representing orientation with Euler angles is compact and readable but can suffer gimbal lock, where one degree of freedom is lost for a particular alignment. Unit quaternions encode rotation without that singularity and allow interpolation along a rotation path, but and represent the same orientation. The 2021 hierarchy lecture mentions the quaternion double-cover issue while discussing rotation and IK MITG-05 (00:25:00–00:45:00). This is a reminder that representation choices have side effects: a representation that makes composition easy may need care when interpolating or enforcing continuity.

A kinematic chain records rigid transforms and joint degrees of freedom. A hinge contributes one angle; a ball joint can contribute three rotational degrees of freedom; a slider contributes translation. Each joint may also have limits. The lecture uses a robot end effector to motivate the same problem in character animation and notes that a virtual character can take a pose that would fling a physical robot because the motion curves are not constrained by hardware forces MITG-05 (00:04:12–00:05:48; 00:21:23–00:25:24). Forward kinematics is therefore a deterministic evaluation of a pose, while inverse kinematics is an optional tool for fitting the pose to a target.
Skinning: attach a surface to a moving skeleton

Before the deformation formula, the sixth lecture frames animation as several tools with different jobs. Traditional cel animation separates a painted background from transparent moving layers, and animators draw key poses while “in-betweeners” fill the frames between them. Computer keyframing keeps the same idea: an artist sets important poses, then a time spline interpolates position or joint angles. That spline is a function of time, so its shape controls both the path and the timing. Procedural animation instead computes motion from rules or code, useful for repeated clocks, crowds, or generated road networks. Physically based animation produces secondary motion—cloth, flags, or fluid—that would be tedious to keyframe, though an artist may have less direct control over it. The lecture’s bouncing-ball example highlights squash-and-stretch and anticipation: an appealing animated ball can deform before impact, intentionally violating literal causality to communicate the action. A film can spend many hours rendering one frame; a game must satisfy an interactive frame budget, so the fidelity and control trade-offs differ MITG-06 (00:03:47–00:06:27; 00:20:14–00:25:30; 00:25:34–00:31:27).

Motion capture records a performer’s movement and maps it onto a virtual rig. When the performer and target character have different proportions or joints, the transfer is called retargeting; raw angles cannot simply be copied because they can produce implausible poses on a different skeleton. The lecture also mentions markerless capture and its smoothing, and separates the captured pose stream from the later deformation of the character’s surface MITG-06 (00:42:00–00:47:08). These methods supply motion; skinning solves the distinct geometric question of how a posed skeleton moves the mesh vertices.

A skeleton provides a compact pose; skinning maps that pose to the many vertices of a surface. In linear blend skinning, also called skeleton-subspace deformation, vertex (x) receives a weighted blend of bone transformations:

The inverse bind transform first expresses the vertex in bone ’s bind-pose frame; the current bone transform sends it into the animated pose. The weights say how strongly each bone influences a vertex. A vertex at a joint might be influenced by both adjacent bones; a vertex in the forearm mostly follows that bone. Weights should sum to one so the blend remains normalized. Skinning can transform thousands of vertices using a small set of joint matrices and weights, allowing artists to shape a mesh once and then animate it through the skeleton.

To unpack the formula, let map bone ’s local coordinates into world coordinates in the bind pose, and let map that bone’s local frame into world coordinates in the current pose. The vertex’s bone-local bind coordinate is . Its posed candidate from that bone is . Then blend those candidates:

The inverse bind matrix matters because a bone’s motion is measured relative to its rest placement. If a joint is translated one unit from the model origin, applying only its current transform would rotate a vertex around the origin. Multiplying by first removes the rest placement; applying then moves it with the animated bone. If the current pose equals the bind pose, , so every bone candidate is and the mesh stays exactly in its rest position. This identity is a valuable implementation check.

For a simple numerical example in 2D homogeneous coordinates, take a rest vertex and a bone whose bind transform is . Its bone-local coordinate is . If the posed bone transform is , then : the point has rotated about the bone origin at , not about the model origin. With two bones, calculate each posed candidate this way first, then blend the resulting points using their weights.

Linear blend skinning is fast because each vertex needs a small number of matrix-vector products, but averaging rotations can shrink the mesh. Let a point be and let two bones rotate it by and around the same joint. The candidate points are and . Equal weights produce

The point collapses onto the joint even though neither bone transform collapses anything. Along a real elbow or wrist this appears as volume loss or a twisting “candy-wrapper” pinch. More weights or smoother interpolation do not remove the underlying issue: a weighted average of rotation matrices need not be a rotation matrix. Common improvements include dual-quaternion blending for rigid motions, additional corrective shapes, or artist-authored weight adjustments; each trades extra machinery or authoring work for better shape preservation. MITG-06 (00:47:17–00:51:00)

The 2021 skinning lecture separates the artist-authored character, the skeleton pose, and the deformation caused by changing pose. It discusses how the surface follows a moving joint, and uses interpolated sensor/pose information as an example of estimating motion between samples MITG-06 (00:05:00–00:30:00; 00:35:00–00:55:00). The important weakness of ordinary matrix blending is that a weighted sum of rigid rotations is generally not itself a rigid rotation. Near joints, this can shrink or twist volume, producing the “candy-wrapper” or collapsing-joint artifact. Dual-quaternion skinning provides one alternative for blending rigid transforms, while corrective shapes or nonlinear methods handle artist-specific deformations. These later options address the limits of the simple baseline rather than making the baseline useless: linear blend skinning is fast, easy to implement, and often adequate when the rig and weights are designed with its behavior in mind.

Hierarchical modeling: reuse geometry through transforms

A scene is easier to build from reusable pieces than from one long list of hard-coded world coordinates. The lecture’s 1977-era Midas example treats a text file as a small modeling program. A polygon command defines a unit square. A transform command moves or rotates it; a create command makes a transformed copy while keeping the source; an extrude command sweeps a face into side polygons; an assemble command combines named pieces. Six instances of a square, each with its own transform, make the six faces of a cube. Repeating the cube with translations creates a larger regular arrangement. (P3-11)

This command list naturally forms a directed graph. The leaf stores the original points; each parent stores which children to include and the transform to apply. A table can reuse one cube model for four legs and a top, changing only each instance’s transform. In a row-vector system, define clearly whether a local transform is applied before or after its parent transform; a child’s world transform is the ordered product along the path from leaf to root. In the column-vector convention, that product order reverses. The same parent-child rule makes an articulated character work: rotate the torso and all descendant parts follow; rotate the upper arm and the forearm follows, while the hand remains attached at its own joint. (P3-11)

The source examples reinforce two useful modeling habits. First, identify repeated structure: many chairs, floor tiles, railroad boards, or background houses can be instances of a few models. Second, keep geometry local and move instances with transforms. This lowers authoring effort and makes the model easier to edit. A graph can be a strict tree, or a DAG if geometry resources are shared; distinguish shared immutable shape data from per-instance transform/material state so changing one chair does not accidentally change every chair. The 2009 fixed-function matrix stack offers push/pop for nested transforms. Current renderers usually traverse an explicit scene graph and pass composed matrices to shaders, but the composition idea is the same. (P3-11)
Animation curves and motion paths
Motion paths and animation curves describe how poses vary through time and how smoothly cameras or characters move.
A camera path is animation plus a frame choice

A camera path specifies position , viewing direction, and an up vector. Interpolating position alone does not define orientation. The view direction must remain normalized; the up vector must avoid becoming parallel to it, or the camera frame becomes singular. One approach interpolates position and orientation separately, using a quaternion for orientation, then reconstructs a camera basis at each time. This camera-path example links animation curves, 3D rotations, and coordinate frames. CMU-20 · CMU-06
Camera orientation continuity along a spline path

A camera path must interpolate both position and orientation while maintaining a valid up direction. A curve can be smooth in position yet rotate abruptly if orientation is interpolated inconsistently. The camera therefore combines geometric curve design, a rotation representation, and time parameterization; its valid orientation frame is part of the animation state. CMU-20

Animation, dynamics, optimization, and PDEs

Animation makes scene state change over time. Keyframes specify selected values, and interpolation fills the intervals. Position often lies in Euclidean space; orientations lie on a curved space, such as the unit quaternion sphere, so componentwise interpolation can take a poor path. Cubic splines use polynomial segments and control continuity: positional continuity means segments meet, tangent continuity means velocities agree, and higher continuity constrains acceleration. Smoothness and temporal coherence matter as much as matching endpoints. CMU-20

Animation has long used sequences of still images to suggest movement. A spinning phenakistoscope hides the changing disc behind a slit so each drawing appears as a separate snapshot rather than a blur. Muybridge’s photographs answered whether all four horse legs leave the ground during a gallop. Digital animation continues this pattern: a new display or computer changes how artists can construct and show motion. The perceptual explanation is not simply that an image lingers on the retina. The brain compares successive visual events and anticipates likely movement (the beta and phi phenomena); a flashing pattern can therefore make equal-speed objects appear to move differently. These cues help explain why the timing and spacing of animated frames matter. CMU-20

Hand-drawn production assigns key poses to a senior animator and fills the intervening drawings with assistants. Computer keyframing applies the same division to scene parameters: key values can be position, color, light intensity, camera zoom, or the degrees of freedom in a character rig. A bouncing ball, for example, may have keys at launch, ground contact, and successive rises and falls. The computer interpolates the parameter values between these events. This saves repetitive work, but the interpolation rule determines the perceived motion. CMU-20

Motion can also come from measurements or rules. Motion capture records reflective markers from multiple cameras and triangulates their 3D positions over time; the resulting joint motion can drive another character’s rig. Procedural animation computes motion from equations, with physical simulation as one example. In a hierarchical rig, transformations form a tree, and splines animate its joint angles and translations. Inverse kinematics reverses the usual question: specify a hand or tool target and solve for the joint angles that place the end effector there, typically as an optimization problem. Skeletal animation deforms a mesh by blending the transformed positions supplied by several bones. Each mesh vertex has weights that indicate the influence of each bone; linear blend skinning averages those transformed positions. This can collapse volume at elbows or shoulders, motivating more physical deformation models. Blend shapes store alternate vertex configurations—such as happy, sad, sleepy, or awake facial poses—and animate time-varying weights for those shapes. Splines can interpolate those weights. CMU-20

PDEs describe fields changing over space and time. The heat equation diffuses temperature toward neighborhood averages. The wave equation propagates disturbances. Initial conditions define the starting field; boundary conditions constrain the domain edge. Dirichlet conditions prescribe the field value; Neumann conditions prescribe flux or derivative. Many physical shapes also minimize an energy functional. The Euler-Lagrange equation gives the stationarity condition; discretizing the field turns that continuous problem into a finite optimization problem. ODE integration and stability

An ordinary differential equation specifies the derivative of a state. If state obeys , explicit Euler advances by . Its local truncation error is proportional to and accumulated global error is generally proportional to . Halving the time step roughly doubles work while often reducing error by about a factor of two. Higher-order Runge-Kutta methods sample the derivative several times per step to improve accuracy.

Stability is distinct from accuracy. A method may have small one-step error but amplify it over repeated steps. For a damped oscillator or stiff spring, explicit Euler becomes unstable if the step is too large relative to the natural frequency. Implicit Euler evaluates at the next state and requires solving an equation, but it can remain stable for much larger steps. Symplectic Euler updates momentum-like variables before positions and often preserves the qualitative energy behavior of mechanical systems. No method is best for all tasks: real-time games may favor predictable cost, offline simulation may favor accuracy, and stiff material models may need implicit solves. CMU-21

Constraints such as fixed joints or nonpenetration conditions restrict the state to a feasible set. A solver can project a tentative update back onto that set or use Lagrange multipliers to introduce constraint forces. The numerical step must respect these conditions; otherwise joints stretch or objects interpenetrate. Time integration, collision queries, and optimization therefore interact in physically based animation. CMU-12 · CMU-21 · CMU-23
Motion models from a tossed rock to crowds

For a rock of mass under gravity , Newton’s second law gives . The acceleration is constant, so position is a parabola in time. A pendulum adds a geometric constraint: the bob moves on a circle and gravitational force is projected onto its tangent direction. A double pendulum couples two angles and can show complex, sensitive motion despite simple equations. These examples show that nonlinear behavior can arise from constraints and coupling, not only from exotic forces.

The same simulation framework extends to flocking, crowds, particle fluids, granular materials, molecular dynamics, cosmological particles, mass-spring systems, and hair. A spring connecting positions with rest length exerts force according to its extension and stiffness. The resulting ordinary differential equations may be stiff when springs are very strong. Crowds add collision avoidance and bottleneck questions; flocking adds local alignment, cohesion, and separation rules. Physical and behavioral models share state integration but differ in the forces or rules driving state change. CMU-21
Keep physical and numerical error separate

An image can look wrong for several distinct reasons. The scene model can be wrong, the chosen physical model can omit effects, the discretization can be coarse, the estimator can have high variance, or the display transform can be inappropriate. These errors should not be conflated. More samples reduce Monte Carlo variance but do not repair a biased material model. More mesh triangles reduce geometric discretization error but do not fix a bad camera. A correct linear-light solution can still look unexpected when mapped into a limited display gamut. A stable simulation can solve the wrong PDE if boundary conditions were encoded incorrectly.

When diagnosing a result, identify the mathematical target first. For rasterization, is the target pixel area coverage or a single center sample? For a light integral, is the measure solid angle or area? For geometry processing, is the target a smooth surface, a discrete mesh, or preserved topology? For animation, should the curve match only positions or also velocities? For optimization, are constraints part of the problem or just penalties? Good questions reveal which error source must be addressed. This precision is the common thread across the course’s rendering, imaging, geometry, and animation topics.

A model can be simple locally and rich globally

Particle systems illustrate a useful modeling pattern: give each element a small state and simple local rules, then let interactions produce a large-scale phenomenon. A particle’s state typically includes position and velocity. A flocking agent can experience three forces: attraction toward a nearby group’s center, separation from neighbors that are too close, and alignment toward their average velocity. These rules are a model of motion, not a claim that the simulation contains a complete psychology of birds or people. They can still reproduce recognizable group motion or estimate where a crowd may bottleneck during evacuation.

The same representation appears at very different scales. Particle interactions approximate fluid motion; contact and friction rules produce granular motion such as sand or popcorn; atom-scale forces support molecular dynamics; gravitational interactions model stars or dark matter. A naive all-pairs force calculation costs roughly interactions for particles. Hierarchical approaches such as Barnes–Hut or the fast multipole method group distant particles and approximate their combined influence, reducing work for appropriate spatial distributions. For sufficiently dense fluids or elastic materials, a continuum model may be a better description: it assigns fields such as velocity and density at every point and expresses their evolution with partial differential equations.

The spring force pulls the endpoints toward the rest length; differentiating the energy gives its direction and magnitude. A mesh can turn this small rule into cloth: each vertex is a particle, edges connect springs, and some vertices can be pinned to a moving character. Hair strands can be chains of particles joined by springs. These models need collision detection and collision response as well: otherwise a cloth point may pass through a character’s body. Their simplicity is attractive, but spring networks can become stiff when springs strongly resist stretching. That stiffness is exactly where integration choices matter. CMU-21

A short coupled-simulation example

Take two particles connected by a spring. Their state is positions and velocities . Spring direction is the normalized displacement from one particle to the other; extension is current length minus rest length . Hooke’s law applies force proportional to extension, with equal and opposite forces on the two particles. Gravity adds another force. Each time step computes forces, converts them to acceleration by dividing by mass, updates velocities, and advances positions. A large spring stiffness creates a high natural frequency, which makes explicit integration require small time steps. If particles also collide, closest-point or distance queries identify contact, and contact forces or projection enforce nonpenetration. The example combines vector calculus, geometry queries, ODE integration, and numerical stability without changing the basic state-update framework. CMU-12 · CMU-21

A cloth mesh needs more than the visible triangle edges

A grid cloth has particles at lattice sites. Structural springs join immediate horizontal and vertical neighbors, resisting stretch. Shear springs join diagonal corners of each cell, resisting in-plane skew. Flexion (or bending) springs link vertices two cells apart, penalizing folds over a wider stencil. The 1995 model discussed in lecture uses these three families. Its diagonal triangulation example exposes anisotropy: if the mesh is triangulated in only one diagonal direction, folding along one edge can change no spring length, while folding along the other diagonal compresses many springs. The resulting stiffness depends on arbitrary tessellation direction rather than just fabric. Adding shear and flexion springs makes a sparse practical model more directionally balanced, though it remains a hand-designed network rather than a full continuum law. MITG-08 (01:06:00–01:11:00)

Substitution into the future acceleration equation yields a sparse linear system for the unknown acceleration (or velocity increment), with matrix terms involving , , and . The exact signs depend on whether force Jacobians are defined as derivatives of force or positive stiffness; use one convention consistently. The computational benefit is that a stiff spring’s fast mode is treated in the solve instead of being chased by tiny explicit steps. The cost is assembling and solving a coupled system. The lecture motivates backward Euler for stiff cloth and identifies the solve as the price of stability; this linearization spells out that mechanism. MITG-08 (00:47:00–00:56:00; 01:12:00–01:16:00)

An ordinary spring chain also cannot model every material property. Hair may need curvature and twist states; twisting an elastic rod can cause it to buckle, a behavior a chain of point masses and length springs cannot express. Discrete elastic rods augment centerline positions with material-frame twist. Real fabric likewise has thickness, weave, friction, bending stiffness, and collision behavior. A simple spring mesh is useful because it chooses a manageable subset. MITG-08 (00:59:00–01:06:40; 01:11:00–01:12:10)
Contact dynamics with a nonintersection guarantee
Connect to: mesh geometry and deformation; numerical optimization; finite-element dynamics; collision detection; friction.

Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) addresses a difficult guarantee: an elastic mesh should not pass through itself, an obstacle, or itself invert between time samples. The method solves each implicit time step by minimizing an incremental action that combines inertial, elastic, and external-force terms. It treats admissible motion as a trajectory through configurations that stay intersection-free. This distinction matters: checking only that the two endpoints of a time step do not overlap can miss a collision that happened in between.

The CCD guarantee preserves feasibility from an admissible starting configuration. If the elastic model also forbids inversion, the initial state must satisfy that condition as well. For a set of nonadjacent surface primitive pairs, compute unsigned distances . A trajectory is intersection-free when these distances stay positive for every time in the step. The admissible set is defined as the closure of the intersection-free trajectories: a motion that just touches and turns away is a limit of valid motions, but a motion that crosses through a surface is not. This definition handles surface obstacles, curves, and points in one framework. It is stronger than merely demanding a nonnegative unsigned distance at the endpoints.
The method adds a localized barrier to the incremental potential. Let be the user-set contact-distance accuracy. For , the barrier is
and it is zero when . It rises without bound as approaches zero, but vanishes for pairs farther apart than the target distance. The barrier-augmented potential is

where is the time-step potential and adjusts barrier stiffness. The clamping is smooth enough for Newton optimization, and distant pairs need no barrier evaluation. The chosen controls geometric accuracy; the solver adapts to balance force strength against conditioning. Too small a allows surfaces to get unnecessarily close before the barrier repels; too large a value makes the system stiff.

The barrier by itself does not guarantee that a numerical descent step stays valid. A Newton direction can pass through a collision and land in a lower-energy configuration on the other side. IPC uses a collision-aware line search: continuous collision detection (CCD) finds an upper bound on the step before any primitive pair intersects; then backtracking reduces the step until the potential decreases. For noninverting elastic models, an inversion-aware limit is combined with the collision limit. This is the mechanism behind the paper’s intersection-free trajectory claim. Floating-point CCD is used in the solver; the authors ran slower exact rational CCD afterward on selected difficult examples as a check, and report that rational CCD was roughly 30 times slower.

The Newton solver projects local elasticity and barrier Hessians to positive semidefinite form before assembly. The assembled system is then positive definite with the inertial mass contribution. Each iteration solves a linear system, takes a CCD-limited descent step, rebuilds the nearby contact set, and repeats until a velocity-scaled step tolerance is met. The paper measures momentum-balance accuracy through the optimization residual. Barrier derivatives yield nonnegative contact-force magnitudes ; a force is applied only within the selected contact distance. This gives an -complementarity condition: force-bearing pairs must be within of contact.

The barrier needs accurate distance derivatives. A vertex-triangle distance and an edge-edge distance each have several closest-point cases: vertex-to-vertex, point-to-edge, or interior projection. Each active case has a closed-form distance function and analytic derivatives. The method stores the active case with its culled contact set. At parallel edge-edge configurations, the ordinary distance function is not differentiable. IPC multiplies the edge-edge barrier by a smooth mollifier that fades it out near parallel degeneracy. Point-triangle pairs remain available to prevent missing collisions. This smoothing protects Newton convergence without claiming that the raw distance formula is smooth at every configuration.
Friction inside the same solve

Coulomb friction depends on the normal contact force and opposes tangential sliding. At a contact pair, write the relative tangential displacement as , where gives a two-dimensional tangent basis. The sliding velocity is . Under the maximal dissipation principle, friction uses the largest opposing force allowed by . This law is difficult for Newton’s method because it switches nonsmoothly between sliding and sticking, and the force depends on the yet-unknown contact reaction.

IPC smooths the force near zero sliding speed with a user-controlled velocity tolerance . Then, within a nonlinear solve, it lags the tangent basis and normal force at values from the preceding iterate. With those quantities held fixed, the smoothed friction force becomes the gradient of a scalar dissipative potential. The method minimizes the barrier-augmented potential plus this lagged friction potential, then updates the basis and contact force and solves again. This is a practical variational approximation: the geometric contact and the frozen friction potential fit in one Newton framework. The authors do not guarantee convergence of every lagged force/basis update in all settings, so that limitation should be retained.
What the paper tests

The paper reports simulations of thin elastic rods and mats, card houses, arches, high-speed ball impact, funnel and point/edge obstacles, large mass and stiffness ratios, and persistent chains of contact. It reports no tunneling at speeds up to 1000 m/s for its ball-and-thin-board example, intersection-free high-speed tests, and stable 100-link chains. Its friction tests recover the expected threshold: a block on a slope stays still when and slides when for the chosen slope. It also demonstrates stick-slip oscillation and contact with codimensional obstacles. Most experiments used CPU sparse direct solvers; the largest “squishy ball” example used AMGCL. Runtime and memory therefore depend on the paper’s mesh size, time step, solver, hardware, and convergence tolerances.

The paper compares IPC with graphics and engineering codes, then implements several sequential quadratic programming (SQP) contact approaches in a common benchmark. The authors report that the compared methods often need small time steps or large contact offsets to avoid failure, while IPC succeeds on their chosen tests. This is evidence about those methods, settings, and benchmark examples. It is not a proof that every contact solver fails or that IPC is inexpensive at arbitrary mesh scale. Cost still rises with resolution and active contacts; exact rational CCD is expensive; friction updates are lagged; and solving the barrier system may be poorly conditioned under extreme deformation.
Source: Li et al., “Incremental Potential Contact: Intersection- and Inversion-free, Large-Deformation Dynamics” (2020), complete paper body and conclusion, PDF pp. 1–20. Primary PDF.

Chapter.Content: Optimization, constraints, and inverse kinematics
Optimization makes inverse problems explicit: define variables, constraints, objectives, and derivative information.
Inverse kinematics as constrained optimization

Inverse kinematics asks for joint parameters that place an end effector at a target. Forward kinematics multiplies transforms along a skeleton chain to map joint angles to hand position. Inverse kinematics reverses that relationship: find joint variables whose forward result matches the target while satisfying joint limits or pose preferences. Define objective . Its gradient uses the kinematic Jacobian. A damped least-squares update avoids unstable large joint motion near singular configurations. Multiple poses can reach the same target, so regularization can prefer a natural pose or smaller change from the current configuration. This is an optimization problem embedded in a transform hierarchy. CMU-05 · CMU-22
Feasibility, constraints, and optimality

An optimization problem has a domain of possible parameters, an objective to minimize, and possibly constraints. A feasible point satisfies every constraint. If two constraints have no common solution, the problem is infeasible; no optimizer can find an answer that satisfies both. For an unconstrained differentiable objective, a local minimum generally has zero gradient, and a twice-differentiable minimum has positive-semidefinite Hessian. Under constraints, these conditions change: the gradient need not be zero because motion may be blocked by a boundary. Lagrange multipliers combine objective and active constraints into stationarity equations.

Convexity means every local minimum is global. A quadratic objective with positive-semidefinite Hessian is convex. Convexity is valuable because optimization guarantees become stronger; nonconvex graphics problems such as camera pose, shape recovery, and neural rendering can have many local minima. Starting points and parameterization matter. CMU-22
Quadratic objectives and linear systems

A least-squares problem has residual vector and objective . Differentiation yields gradient ; setting it to zero gives normal equations . If columns of are nearly dependent, the system is poorly conditioned and small data changes can cause large parameter changes. QR or SVD factorization can solve least squares more stably than directly forming normal equations. The connection between optimization and numerical linear algebra is direct: the objective’s geometry is encoded in matrix conditioning. CMU-02 · CMU-22

Newton’s method locally approximates the objective with a quadratic and solves , where is the Hessian. For a true quadratic objective, one exact Newton step reaches the minimizer if is invertible. For nonlinear objectives, the Hessian changes, so line searches or trust regions limit step size. Quasi-Newton methods estimate curvature from gradients and avoid explicitly forming a large Hessian. Gradient descent is cheaper per step but may require many iterations in a narrow valley. CMU-22
Differentiating through a graphics pipeline

If an image depends on shape, camera, or material parameters, define loss . The chain rule propagates derivatives through transformations, projection, interpolation, shading, and compositing. Some operations are smooth, such as matrix multiplication; others are discontinuous, such as visibility changes at an edge. Derivative-based optimization can struggle at visibility boundaries because a tiny parameter change suddenly reveals or hides a surface. This motivates soft visibility approximations, gradient estimators, or alternative objectives. The same derivative machinery used for simple curve fitting therefore reaches inverse graphics and data fitting. CMU-03 · CMU-22
Feasible sets, existence, and the difference between local and global

A useful standard form is: choose a parameter vector to minimize an objective subject to inequalities . The objective assigns a cost to each candidate; the constraints determine which candidates are allowed. A maximization can be written as minimization by negating the score. An equality can be encoded by two inequalities, and . For example, maximize the area enclosed by a curve while fixing its perimeter. The circle solves this classical isoperimetric problem, but the optimization setup is simply “minimize negative area subject to the perimeter constraint.”

Before searching for a minimum, check whether an allowed point exists. That is feasibility. Contradictory requirements such as and leave no feasible point; a solver cannot satisfy both. Even when a feasible point exists, a minimum need not be attained. The function over the whole real line decreases without bound, so there is no smallest value. The function is bounded below by zero but approaches zero only as ; no finite attains it. Sufficient existence conditions include a continuous objective over a nonempty compact feasible set (closed and bounded), or a coercive objective on a closed feasible set, where “coercive” means the cost grows toward as the parameter moves arbitrarily far away.

A global minimum is no worse than every feasible alternative. A local minimum is no worse than candidates in a small neighborhood. The two can differ: pulling a string tight along a path tangled around buildings can produce a locally shortened path that is still globally much longer than a direct route. Multiple global minima are possible too. In the lecture’s visualization, minimizing over the unit disk gives two equal optima, and . Global search can be expensive, so many practical graphics methods seek a useful local solution and depend on initialization.

For a differentiable unconstrained function, a local minimum must have zero gradient: to first order, no direction can reduce the value. But this only identifies a critical point, which may also be a maximum or saddle. The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives and describes local curvature. At a twice-differentiable local minimum it must be positive semidefinite, meaning for every direction . A bowl passes this test; a saddle has a direction with negative curvature. With active constraints, the unconstrained gradient need not vanish: the lowest point of a bowl restricted to a boundary can have a slope pointing outside the allowed region. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions add multipliers for active constraints and encode that balance. CMU-22
Convexity and why quadratic energy often reduces to linear algebra

A set is convex if the straight segment between any two points in it stays inside it. A function is convex if its graph lies below every chord joining two points on the graph. This rules out hidden bowls separated by hills: every local minimum of a convex function is global. Strong convexity adds curvature in every direction and gives a unique minimum. These properties make convex problems attractive in geometry processing, image processing, and animation, though “convex” alone does not guarantee every large problem is cheap.
A central example is a quadratic objective

where is a vector of unknowns, is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, and is a fixed vector. The gradient is and the Hessian is . Setting the gradient to zero yields . Thus a linear system with a positive semidefinite matrix is also the condition for the bottom of a convex quadratic bowl. If is positive definite, the bowl curves upward in every direction and the minimizer is unique. If is only semidefinite, the bowl may be flat along some directions, so many points can achieve the same minimum. If is indefinite, the graph has saddle directions and may fall without bound. The quadratic error used to choose a mesh-collapse position is one graphics example of this structure. CMU-22
Gradient descent, step control, and curvature
Gradient descent is a repeated local improvement rule. At a candidate , the gradient points toward steepest increase, so a small move in the opposite direction decreases the objective:

The positive step length determines how far to travel. This update is forward Euler applied to the gradient-flow differential equation . The connection explains why step size matters: a huge step can overshoot and jump around the objective; a tiny step makes slow progress. A line search tests candidate lengths and selects one that decreases the objective while meeting sufficient-decrease and curvature conditions, such as Armijo–Wolfe conditions. A small fixed step is simpler but can waste iterations or fail on poorly scaled problems.

The method follows only the slope at the current point. In a long, narrow valley, the steep direction across the valley can dominate the gradient even though progress toward the minimum is along the valley. Repeated steps zigzag across it. Newton’s method uses the Hessian to scale directions according to curvature:

This is obtained by minimizing a local quadratic approximation of the objective. Near a well-behaved minimum it can converge much faster than gradient descent. However, an indefinite Hessian can direct a step toward a saddle instead of a minimum, and computing or solving with a full Hessian may be costly. Quasi-Newton methods such as L-BFGS approximate curvature from gradients; trust-region methods limit the update to a neighborhood where the local approximation is credible. There is no universal optimizer for all nonconvex graphics problems; objective structure, scaling, initialization, constraints, and prior experience guide the choice. CMU-22
Function spaces and image error
Vectors need not be finite coordinate lists. A function can be treated as a vector in a function space. For image functions , an inner product can be . Its induced norm is

This measures total squared difference across an image domain. A discrete image approximates the integral with a sum over pixels. The distinction between a continuous field and its finite samples matters: changing pixel resolution changes the discrete sum unless sample spacing or area weights are handled correctly. Function-space gradients are functions too. For objective , the functional derivative is ; at every point it says whether the image is too bright or too dark relative to target. This is the continuous analogue of an ordinary least-squares gradient. CMU-02 · CMU-03 · CMU-22
Automatic differentiation

Automatic differentiation computes derivatives by applying the chain rule to the arithmetic operations in a program. A value can be paired with its derivative; addition and multiplication propagate both. If , then derivative with respect to a parameter is . This differs from finite differences, which estimate a derivative by evaluating nearby values and can suffer cancellation or step-size error. It also differs from symbolic differentiation, which transforms an expression into a new symbolic formula. In graphics optimization, automatic differentiation can produce gradients through complex energy computations, though discrete visibility changes and branching still require care. CMU-21 · CMU-22
Computing derivatives: four different contracts

A simulation or optimizer often needs a derivative of a complicated energy with respect to thousands of positions. The derivative is not merely a formula: the method used to obtain it has its own accuracy and cost contract.
Finite differences perturb one input and compare two outputs. For scalar , a forward difference is

This works even when is a black box, which is why it is useful for debugging and checking a derivative implementation. But choosing is delicate. A large step measures an average slope over a nonlocal interval (truncation error); a tiny step subtracts nearly equal floating-point numbers, losing significant digits through cancellation. In many dimensions, estimating every component this way may require one or more function evaluations per input variable.

Automatic differentiation carries derivative information through the operations the program performs. In forward mode, a scalar is paired with its value and derivative, . For a product , the product rule gives . For instance, initialize , where the second component means . Multiplying it by itself gives ; multiplying by a constant gives , the value and derivative of at . This computes derivatives to floating-point precision without selecting a perturbation size. It requires arithmetic types that propagate derivatives. Forward mode is especially natural when there are few inputs; reverse mode is advantageous for many inputs and a small number of outputs, which is common when differentiating one scalar loss with respect to many parameters.

Symbolic differentiation transforms an expression tree into a new tree for its derivative. Once built, the derivative expression can be evaluated repeatedly. Symbolic tools are helpful for algebra and analysis, but repeated chain-rule expansion can create very long formulas, especially for vector and matrix expressions. The result may be mathematically correct yet obscure a simple geometric structure.

Geometric differentiation asks what perturbation changes the quantity and by how much. For a triangle with fixed edge vector as base and a moving opposite vertex , area is , where is the perpendicular height. Moving parallel to changes neither the base nor height, so the gradient has no component along . Moving it one unit in the height-increasing direction changes area by , so the gradient’s magnitude is half the base length and its direction is perpendicular to . In 3D, if is the oriented unit normal, that direction is given up to sign by ; the sign depends on which triangle vertex moves and the orientation convention. This compact answer is easier to reason about than an expanded symbolic formula. The gradient points toward fastest increase; for potential energy , the corresponding conservative force is , pointing toward decreasing potential. CMU-21
